Interviewer:	I’ll start off telling you a bit about our project. We’re interviewing 2nd year women students that are going on placement (right). We want to interview them about their expectations of the placement are and about their experience of higher education so far and also their career aspirations and what they want to do. We’re hoping to interview students again while they’re on their placements and again afterwards (oh right). At the end of it we will put together a document, that we’re going to give to the Engineering Council and hopefully it will help to improve the situation for women (yeah) in the engineering industry.

Subject:	Ah, right, because it’s always a struggle isn’t it?

Interviewer:	So if I can just start off asking you a bit of background information.

Subject:	Right, yeah that’s fine.

Interviewer:	How old are you?

Subject:	I’m 20.

Interviewer:	20. Did you come straight from (yeah) school?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Can you just remind me what course you’re doing?

Subject:	I’m doing a BSc in energy and environmental technologies.

Interviewer:	Did you do ‘A’ levels?

Subject:	No, I did a BTec in Engineering. National Diploma

Interviewer:	Right, did you do that here or…?

Subject:	No I did that at [college], at home.

Interviewer:	OK, was that at a college did you say?

Subject:	Yeah, it was a college of technology.

Interviewer:	Ok, and what type of school did you go to before that?

Subject:	I went to a country school, in the middle of nowhere really.

Interviewer:	Yeah – was it an all girls school?

Subject:	No, no, mixed.

Interviewer:	OK. Have you got any previous work experience in the industry at all?

Subject:	In the industry? No not really.

Interviewer:	That’s alright. Are either of your parents engineers at all?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Ok, so when and why do you think you decided to be an engineer?

Subject:	I did a WISE course (oh right) in my last year at school, and I was umming and aahing about whether to go into erm I was sort of debating what to do, whether to go into ‘A’ levels and I thought, oh I enjoy this, so I went on and did the engineering straight from school. (yeah) Erm, but I didn’t really know what I wanted to do (yeah) I thought oh, I’ll go in – maybe energy, sort of energy production, but apart from that I wasn’t really sure what I was doing. And then I just sort of progressed to sort of looking for energy related degree courses, I suppose and there wasn’t – there isn’t that many, there’s only about 20 odd in the country and half of them are up in Scotland. And I was like no, I don’t want to go all the way up there – too far. Erm, so I decided to go – it was sort of a decision between Leeds and here. (right) So I thought well, being as it was quite a long way if I wanted to come home – it was a bit of a trek, so I decided to come here.

Interviewer:	OK. Did you ever consider any of the other types of engineering at all?

Subject:	Erm, I nearly did before I got my erm placement at – at college to do a BTec in engineering. I was offered erm an apprenticeship in electronics, erm at – which was sort of connected with another college at home and erm they – and I was like do I want to specialise straight away or do I sort of get a general – and I thought oh I’ll go for a general overview and then it was like sort of umming and aahing about other things, because I nearly considered joining the services as well – doing engineering through them. I was like, oh, I don’t know what to do, you know, so it was sort of a bit up in the air.

Interviewer:	When you decided to do the BTec, did you know that you wanted to go to university or was it while you were doing that, that you decided?

Subject:	I think it was while I was doing it really. Erm, I thought well I can only get so far without a degree, especially in engineering. I was like oh I might as well go and do it then – go to University. But it was quite interesting because it was like – everyone thought oh, you do ‘A’ levels, and then you do – go into University – yeah, so it sort of – and UCAS were in a bit of a nightmare in that sense (really) because they hadn’t not – they’d sort of adapted the UCAS – they’ve got a points system to get in and they’d adapted their system to get into through ‘A’ level students and points and everything like that, and they’d done Scottish highers and everything like that – mention a BTec and they’re like what? Right, well we haven’t a clue how many points for that and so a lot of Universities are like oh, don’t like BTec’s – a bit sort of oh dear.

Interviewer:	Did you ever consider doing ‘A’ levels?

Subject:	I did, briefly, but I thought I prefer doing course work and I’m not – I thought well I’m not so strong at exams, so I thought well I’ll do – I prefer to do a B – a course work based one – because I didn’t actually have to sit any exams for the BTec.

Interviewer:	That sounds good.

Subject:	Yes, it’s lovely.

Interviewer:	What is it then, that appeals to you about engineering?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know. (laughs) Erm, I’ve just sort of fallen into it. It’s quite interesting and quite systematic. I like problem solving and things like that. (Yeah) I don’t know.

Interviewer:	That’s OK. Did you always know that you wanted to do a sandwich course?

Subject:	Yeah. Yeah, I thought well erm I’ve got no experience (yeah) of the industry so I was compl – especially on my course, there’s – well, I’m the only one actually doing my degree but there’s sort of 3 other degrees very similar and I was the only – I’m the youngest by about 5 years on it. So the average age is about 35 I’d say, so they’ve all come out of industry, come in doing a degree and then they’ll go back out. And I was like, well, I’m competing against them, at the end of the day, so I thought right…

Interviewer:	Do you think the age thing is maybe why the other people haven’t so much (yeah) gone in to doing the placements because they’ve already got that experience?

Subject:	Yes, and they’ve got families to support and they can’t – they’ve got to get through university as quickly as possible really (Yeah) to erm then be able to go out and back into industry, so…

Interviewer:	OK, when you decided to do engineering did you realise that it was so male dominated?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	And does it bother you at all?

Subject:	No it doesn’t. It’s never sort of been an issue. Erm, I mean I was the only – on my – doing the engineering at college, I was the only girl doing that (yeah) and I knew – and it was quite funny because the lect – all the lecturers were like – they were all old school engineers and they’d start swearing and turn around and say what the heck are you doing, sort of thing. And then they’d say, ooh sorry there and they’d apologise to you and I’m like, why? Why are you apologising? And erm I think in some ways it’s like – and they were all – or they’d say oh close your ears Suzanne and have a go. Which I found was quite amusing but in some ways it’s sort of a bit prejudicial – it’s like yeah, I’m no different to them really. Yeah, it was quite funny.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that more women should be encouraged to go into engineering?

Subject:	Definitely – yeah, because it’s such a big field, I don’t see why it should be so male dominated.

Interviewer:	Yeah. What do you think could be done to encourage more women into engineering?

Subject:	Awareness (yeah) it’s more awareness than anything.

Interviewer:	Knowing what engineering is in the first place?

Subject:	Exactly because people think engineering – they think car work – mechanical. Erm, and there’s so much more about it that they don’t know about and I mean I had an – I mean – I was at – my school we didn’t really get anything coming through erm and it wasn’t sort of a – oh, you should go and do engineering – people didn’t really think about it, to sort of push the girls through, when I think there is a lot of potential out there.

Interviewer:	Yeah, and do you think that WISE thing was quite crucial for you then?

Subject:	Oh yeah – I wouldn’t even have thought about it. I was thinking about going and doing law or something like that. I couldn’t sort of imagined doing engineering.

Interviewer:	What characteristics do you feel make a good engineer?

Subject:	Erm, I think you’ve got to be a sort of quite calm and level headed, erm and systematic in the way you think like problem solving and confident in what they say – yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think any of those characteristics are perceived as more male characteristics or female characteristics?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t think so. I think every – it’s sort of equal – the only thing that I think is erm different, sort of, is the heavy duty sort of eng – is the big, heavy mechanical but if you go through all the degree and everything you’re not likely to go back and do all the heavy manual stuff, it’s more likely to be sort of clean work. (Yes, OK) so that’s the only reason.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are any particular advantages or disadvantages of being a female engineer?

Subject:	Hmm, not really. Erm, no. I mean yeah there’s still a lot of people – sort of talking to people there’s still sort of that old school attitude where women aren’t expected to be in engineering and oh no, what’s going on? Erm, I think that’s sort of the only side of it you’ve got to fight against really to get through and prove yourself and you’ve got – in some ways, going – like hitting that in college, it was something that you sort of realised. And you almost have to work twice as hard as the men to show that you’re perfectly capable of doing exactly the same job. I think, in some ways, it pushes you harder so – and so – almost it’s on – if that’s the case everywhere else, that the women are going to end up becoming better than – better quality.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are any particular advantages to being a woman?

Subject:	Not really.

Interviewer:	I’ve had some people say that they probably get more help in class and stuff like that (yeah, yeah). I don’t know whether people perceive that as good or patronising or…

Subject:	Yeah, it can come across patronising. I can see where they’re coming across that erm but sometimes it was quite nice, especially being sort of erm in the labs doing lathe work and things like that – I did find it useful then – going, yeah, we’ll come and do it for you (laughs)

Interviewer:	OK, has the course then been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	Erm, I’d say yes but it’s totally confused me (yes) because I came in here thinking oh, I’m going to do energy work but there’s quite a lot of environmental and I was a bit sort of prejudicial against it. I was like, oh no, you know, not for me, I’m gonna …and it’s slowly turned me – I’m really confused about what I want to do now. Erm, like I was originally looking for my next year to do a placement within the energy area, sort of energy conservation and things like that erm but I’ve ended up getting a placement in an environmental department (OK). So it’s sort of twisted everything round and I’m like OK, I don’t mind, cos it’s like – I find that I came into the course thinking right I’m gonna come out with an energy based degree and that’s where I’m gonna go – I’m gonna go and work somewhere in that field. And, the environmental thing’s just (sighs) and they said, oh now don’t sort of burn your bridges yet and by the end of the year I was like oh, this environmental stuff isn’t too bad. It’s quite interesting.

Interviewer:	OK what do you think have been the best and the worse things about the course so far?

Subject:	Er, best things? There’s a (lost words) like the range of subjects we cover (yeah) it is so broad. I mean last year we did erm planning – the planning work, sort of building planning – building regulations and we’ve done like health & safety things and erm, and when we go back sort of environmental technologies – sort of chimney designs and landfill like – so I mean it’s very broad and covers everything and anything (laughs) – it’s quite interesting in that sense, although that can be a disadvantage as well (yeah) because it’s like you can’t – a lot of like a lot of the group you have one sort of area, and they’re all interlocked – we’ll have modules – we’ll have one module and another module sort of miles away – and you’re like OK and…yeah, they sort of overlap but miles sort of very briefly (yeah) so it makes sort of revising it and learning it all very difficult in that sense.

Interviewer:	OK, are you pleased that you did decide to choose this course then?

Subject:	Yeah, I am actually. Er, it’s opened my mind up to a lot of things and it’s been very interesting I think.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s good, have you been taught by any female lecturers at all?

Subject:	Yeah. Our Law lecturer is female.

Interviewer:	So they’re not actually in engineering?

Subject:	Erm, no, they’re in environmental though. Our health – our health & safety lecturer she was – she’s female and she’s engineering based (yeah) and who else, yeah, just those two.

Interviewer:	OK–do you find that encouraging having female lecturers? Would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

Subject:	No, I don’t think – it’s like if the subject’s put across in the right way, I don’t see why it should be taught by females…

Interviewer:	Yeah, so it’s the quality of the teaching staff?

Subject:	Yeah, and if it inspires you to go on, I don’t think it should matter.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s fine. Do you think that the female lecturers treat you the same as the male lecturers?

Subject:	Yeah, (yeah?) yeah – there’s no – I wouldn’t say there’s any difference.

Interviewer:	And do the male lecturers treat the male and female students the same?

Subject:	Yeah, I would say so. You know there’s not – because there’s only like 3 of us, it’s not sort of as it – like at college it was, I was treated slightly different but I had – it was all male lecturers. But here there are like the 3 of us all girls and we’re just treated exactly the same as everyone else.

Interviewer:	Why do you think you were treated differently at college?

Subject:	I think it’s all because they’re all old school engineers …

Interviewer:	And they were like my God it’s a girl, how do we teach a girl?

Subject:	Yeah, they haven’t had like – I was – yeah, I was the only person in the school who they had like at school there, who was a girl. And it was – they were like oh OK. Erm, and then – yeah, then there was a girl in the year below me, who came through but it was sort of a bit – a bit like oh right, yeah, OK, fine…

Interviewer:	OK, have you got a personal tutor? 

Subject:	I think so. (laughs). It’s a bit – because there’s only – there’s only 14 of us on the entire 3 degrees, so – and we – all the lecturers are very approachable, so I think I have somewhere along the line but we – if we’ve got a problem we can go and see any of the lecturers (OK, yes, fine) and any lecturer at any time.

Interviewer:	Is there anything or anyone that you’d say has been the biggest influence on you, since you started the course?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	OK, do you have to do a lot of group work?

Subject:	Yes, well this year we have – last year we didn’t really have any but this year about half our course work’s been group work, which makes it – it’s been quite difficult because everyone’s old – older. It’s made – and lives away from the University and there’s quite a long distance (yeah) and so getting together and they’ve got all lives at home or they’ve all got jobs outside, so trying to sort of organise group work is just a bit of a nightmare. So, in that sense it’s quite…

Interviewer:	Yeah – do you think that there are benefits to doing group work?

Subject:	I think there is in some ways in the fact that you get an overall view – you get lots of different people’s ideas and you get – you build on everyone else’s strengths and so in a sense you should come out with a decent piece of work at the end. Erm, that’s if everyone pulls their weight.

Interviewer:	Do you think that it will help you when you do go to work in the industry – the fact that you have had the experience of working with other people?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely. Erm, it makes you build on your patience.

Interviewer:	Do you get to choose who you work with when you work in groups, or do you get put into them?

Subject:	In theory yes, but in practice not really because it sort of all falls into the right – same groups, so it’s not that much of a choice and there’s only a few of us anyway.

Interviewer:	Do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

Subject:	Definitely. Yeah, erm, women will put more detail, and more attention to detail rather than the men will just right, that’s it, that’s fine, go. They’re sort of a bit more slapdash erm and a lot of the women have got a lot more patience I always think than certain men.

Interviewer:	Do you prefer working with the women then, or…?

Subject:	Er, I dunno, I think it makes it more interesting having a sort of mixed group, because it sort of makes life a bit more challenging.

Interviewer:	Have you had any particularly bad experiences of group work then?

Subject:	Erm, I’ve had people not pulling their weight, which is very annoying.

Interviewer:	Yeah. What do you do in that situation?

Subject:	Persuade them and then get to the end as sort of deadlines are nearing and it’s like right, OK, fine, we’ll go and do the work ourselves if it’s not going to happen, because at the end of the day it’s your mark that’s being affected, so it’s very annoying when that happens but you have to sort of deal with it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that any aspects of the teaching or advice that you’ve had will help you when you go on your placement?

Subject:	Er, obviously like the knowledge that they give us (yeah) but I don’t know – no I …

Interviewer:	Do you think that you will get the opportunity to put the skills that you’ve learnt into practice?

Subject:	Hopefully, yeah. And pick up like lots of new skills as well.

Interviewer:	OK, do you feel prepared and ready to go on your placement now?

Subject:	Erm, I think so. There’s still a few things that I’ve got to sort out first. Erm, I think yeah – just about getting there.

Interviewer:	And do the University do anything to help prepare you at all?

Subject:	Erm, no not really. It’s been sort of they – I’ve had to chase them up to sort of do anything.

Interviewer:	Yeah. How, how much of a role do they have in helping you find a placement?

Subject:	Erm, in theory they’re meant to have quite – sort of be there, help you and point you in the right direction, but in practice it’s a bit more OK, so go and find it yourself, although my placement actually – the company wrote to the University and it sort of – I was made aware of it (yeah) that they needed someone, so I just applied for it. Erm, 

Interviewer:	Did anyone particularly encourage or discourage you from going on placement?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t think so. I think like erm I talked it over with lecturers and they like sort of said yes, er so they gave me advice on both sides of the sort of – yes, you can finish it early – your degree early – but in my case, because I’ve come straight through, I’ve got no rush to finish it, sort of thing. Erm, I think one thing which is – like for other people who – that puts them off from doing a placement is financial. Erm, they just can’t afford to, but I think it was always going to be a case that I was going to do a placement (yeah) because I knew I had no experience (yeah) so there’s that to think about.

Interviewer:	Do you think it will improve your career prospects in that respect then?

Subject:	Yeah, especially because it’s a big company – an international company. It’s with [company] rm and so it’s a big company and the site is huge and I’ll be working in a team of I think 6. So, in that respect – and they’ve already said, er when I went for my interview they were like well have you done this, have you done that? I was like no, OK we’ll train you up and we’ll show you how to do it. So I’ll get – hopefully, I’ll be able to get lots of experience and they’ve got lots of different things on site, so they’ve got their own landfill site, they’ve got their own incineration plant and things like that and combined heated power unit as well. So there’s lots to sort of pick up on there.

Interviewer:	And do you have the opportunity to move around within the company?

Subject:	No. I think it will be fairly – cos it’s only – because I’m with the environmental department, it’s going to be fairly restrained but within that – I’ll be able to – I’ll have a year in certain jobs, which is sort of daily jobs and then, but then I’ll be shared between the 6 people so they’ve all got their own little areas, so one’s sort of landfill site – one’s – so I should be able to get a good insight into what goes on and things like that.

Interviewer:	Good. Did you apply to any other companies at all?

Subject:	Erm, I wrote – who did I write to? I wrote to erm I can’t remember what they’re called now. There’s a Government erm energy saving group, which I wrote to and they said they hadn’t decided on what their budget was so they couldn’t afford to – and then I wrote to a few other people – groups like that.

Interviewer:	What were your main criteria for looking for placements? Was it mainly the type of work they did or did you look, like you said at whether they were willing to train you – did you look at things like that?

Subject:	Not really. It was more a case of I needed a placement. I was sort of open to anything by the end of it because I sort of emailed around the companies and there was just nothing (yeah) or they just couldn’t afford to have someone. So, to find a placement was so hard, I was just – I got to the point – cos originally I was like right I’m gonna do energy, I want to do energy (yeah) and it got to the point where I was like well, I don’t mind what I do, if it’s connected. I thought I’ll do it sort of thing. So I was very open in that sense.

Interviewer:	Where are they based?

Subject:	 [Company]? (Yes) Erm, the site which I’m working on is in [town], in [area]. Erm, which is a long way.

Interviewer:	Yes, are you worried about that at all or…?

Subject:	No, not really, because it was one question they asked me, is how did I feel being so far away? And I didn’t mind because I worked in the summer – I spent 3 months in Italy working (oh right) so it’s like the distance I don’t mind. As long as there’s a phone sort of thing (yeah) and I can ring home. Erm, but sort of it doesn’t bother me at all.

Interviewer:	OK, did you do much research into the company when you… ?

Subject:	I did before I went for the interview (yeah) because I sort of sent off my CV just as a sort of off chance, so sort of well oh well, I might as well send it off and I hadn’t even a clue what the company was before, it’s a bit bad of me really. And so – and then I had a letter come through saying oh, can you come for interview? I was like what? So I thought I’d better just see what I’ve applied to (laughs) so yeah, a bit of a shock.

Interviewer:	Is that just like looking on the Internet?

Subject:	Yeah, just see what they do. Yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, would you have liked the University to give you more help in finding a placement?

Subject:	Definitely.

Interviewer:	And what do you think they could have done?

Subject:	I think they could have erm put out more feeders and things (yeah) because I mean yes, we’re only a small group of students but they had about 3 offers, which isn’t a lot.

Interviewer:	Are any of the males on your course going on placement?

Subject:	I think – I think one or two, I’m not sure.

Interviewer:	So there’s very few people going on placement anyway, it’s not just girls?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah – it’s not, no. Yeah, I think there’s only about 3 of us, that are out for the year. Erm, so yeah it’s very – it is hard to find them. It’s like looking for a needle in a haystack sometimes and because it’s – like if you were doing mechanics or something like that erm you’d be able to – there’s a lot of placements out there, but you say energy or environmental and they’re like ooh, no we haven’t got anything. It’s very specialised. Yeah, which makes it harder.

Interviewer:	OK, what are you most looking forward to and most apprehensive about in placement?

Subject:	Er, looking forward to sort of getting hands on experience, learning the new skills, sort of working within an office environment, which I haven’t done really and working with a sort of team which seems to get on really well. I’ve spoke to the erm the trainee who was there, doing the job at the moment and he was like yeah, they’re really sort of good and they’re really supportive and talking to other people who worked at the company they were like erm yeah, it’s – the company’s really good and they’re really sort of – so I’m looking forward to that sort of support network and how it – so it sort of – and all the different things they’ve got on site, presumably it should be interesting to get into. Erm, apprehensive? Not knowing what sort of – the appropriate information, which is a bit daunt – sort of daunting and a bit – you think oh well, they’re paying me all this money to come here and do the placement, so that’s going to be a bit of a (yeah) – a bit scary in some other senses. Erm, but I’m …

Interviewer:	OK, in terms of your career then what do you see yourself doing in say 5 years time?

Subject:	 (laughter) Haven’t got a clue! 

Interviewer:	Do you think that you will you be in the Engineering industry?

Subject:	Loosely connected I think. I have a feeling if I really enjoy this placement, I’ll stay in the environmental side and – but it’s still sort of loosely connected because it’s all the technologies and things like that, sort of pollution controls and things.
Interviewer:	Is that one of the things that you’re hoping to get out the placement as well? (yeah) … helping you decide more what you want to do?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah. Erm, see if I like it – well, fall into something hopefully, but I have a habit of just falling into things. I don’t really plan them it’s like oh yeah, I’ll do that. So I haven’t a clue.

Interviewer:	Ok. What would be your ideal career then?

Subject:	Ideal career – erm, I don’t know.

Interviewer:	Not necessarily in terms of a job but erm …

Subject:	What I want to get out of a job sort of thing?

Interviewer:	Yeah, like do you see yourself going into managerial things or …?

Subject:	Yeah eventually.

Interviewer:	Is location and things like that?

Subject:	Yeah, a nice sort of not really urban area, but a sort of semi-urban – a nice location, erm and a nice sort of friendly atmos – company with sort of working within a team, or managerial post – definitely.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that’s achievable?

Subject:	Yes, eventually (laughs) yeah. A few years experience and then – definitely.

Interviewer:	You said that in terms of placement, there isn’t that much going, do you think that the career prospects are good in your field of engineering, or do you think when you come to look for a job do you think you’ll have the same sort of difficulties?

Subject:	I think like jobs – like finding a job – I think there are the jobs out there erm and they are asking for – like if you look in the sort of journals and things (yeah) there are the jobs advertised and – but they’re wanting more than a year’s experience, so in sort of I’ve got to do this placement to be able to get a job at the end. But there are the jobs, it’s just the fact that a lot of companies don’t like doing the – the sort of erm paying for a place for trainees who come through – that’s the sort of impression that I got (yeah) from the different places that I sort of encountered…

Interviewer:	OK, are you happy with all the career choices you’ve made so far? Would you do anything differently if you had to do it all again?

Subject:	Erm, No, I think it’s sort of – I’ve not been unhappy (yeah) although I probably would have gone to a different college to do the (BTec) BTec – yeah. They were – it’s not the best of places.

Interviewer:	In terms of what?

Subject:	Er, I was spending my time chasing after lecturers to find where my work – if they’d marked it or – and I was like hang on, I shouldn’t be doing this, they should have it done sort of thing (yeah). They were a bit sort of lax in that sense, which was a bit annoying, especially towards the end. And they didn’t sort of give me the guidance that I needed, it was like erm – well you – like applying through UCAS, it was just – I accidentally found out from a friend, ooh, you’re meant to go and apply through UCAS. I wasn’t told a thing, so in that sense it was sort of – that was my only really bad sort of decision I’d say. But I wouldn’t say no to doing a BTec again.

Interviewer:	Did any of the other people that were doing your BTec go to University or were they following a different route?

Subject:	One – there was one other, but I think he dropped out half way through the first year. Erm, they weren’t academically minded, let’s put it that way. I think they all went into – they all found jobs.

Interviewer:	OK, what 5 words would you use to describe sort of your experience of the engineering industry so far?

Subject:	Er, I’d say challenging (yeah) – it can be a bit sort of - a bit stand offish to women. Erm, interesting, erm and complicated because there’s so many different fields that it makes it sort of a bit – you go in and say oh, ok I’ll do engineering – what sort? (Yes) You’re definitely not told at school or anything what the difference – there are so many different fields and you say oh engineering – people are like oh right, OK, they think cars again but they’re like – they’re not – kids aren’t informed that there are all these different little pockets, different areas – it’s so wide.

Interviewer:	Do you think that any of those things might be problematic for you, trying to get into the industry and move forward in the industry, like the fact that it can be stand offish to women?

Subject:	Erm, I think it will make it more of a challenge but – in some senses – but then it males life a bit more interesting in a sort of – yeah, you’ve got to work, you’ve got to prove yourself a bit more.

Interviewer:	Yeah, does that worry you or bother you at all?

Subject:	No (laughs) it’s just another challenge. It’s just another difficulty to overcome. So, no, it just makes it interesting.

Interviewer:	OK. Why do you think that it’s been so masculine – do you think that’s purely to do with (yes) the numbers of males within the industry or is it the type of work as well?

Subject:	I think it’s history (yeah). A lot of it has to do with history, that it’s never been a female area and yeah, the number of men in the industry.

Interviewer:	Do you think the situation for women will improve?

Subject:	I think it will improve very slowly. Erm, it’s just got to sort of gradually pick up the pace a bit. (yeah) But I think it will change in the next sort of 10 to 15 years, I think it will change more and more – become more equal.

Interviewer:	OK that’s everything. Thanks very much that’s been really helpful.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I’ll start off telling you a bit about our project. We’re interviewing 2nd year women students that are going on placement (right). We want to interview them about their expectations of the placement are and about their experience of higher education so far and also their career aspirations and what they want to do. We’re hoping to interview students again while they’re on their placements and again afterwards (oh right). At the end of it we will put together a document, that we’re going to give to the Engineering Council and hopefully it will help to improve the situation for women (yeah) in the engineering industry.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Ah, right, because it’s always a struggle isn’t it?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So if I can just start off asking you a bit of background information.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Right, yeah that’s fine.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How old are you?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: 20. Did you come straight from (yeah) school?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Can you just remind me what course you’re doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’m doing a BSc in energy and environmental technologies.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you do ‘A’ levels?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I did a BTec in Engineering. National Diploma

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Right, did you do that here or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No I did that at [college], at home.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, was that at a college did you say?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, it was a college of technology.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, and what type of school did you go to before that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I went to a country school, in the middle of nowhere really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah – was it an all girls school?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, no, mixed.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Have you got any previous work experience in the industry at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In the industry? No not really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s alright. Are either of your parents engineers at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, so when and why do you think you decided to be an engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I did a WISE course (oh right) in my last year at school, and I was umming and aahing about whether to go into erm I was sort of debating what to do, whether to go into ‘A’ levels and I thought, oh I enjoy this, so I went on and did the engineering straight from school. (yeah) Erm, but I didn’t really know what I wanted to do (yeah) I thought oh, I’ll go in – maybe energy, sort of energy production, but apart from that I wasn’t really sure what I was doing. And then I just sort of progressed to sort of looking for energy related degree courses, I suppose and there wasn’t – there isn’t that many, there’s only about 20 odd in the country and half of them are up in Scotland. And I was like no, I don’t want to go all the way up there – too far. Erm, so I decided to go – it was sort of a decision between Leeds and here. (right) So I thought well, being as it was quite a long way if I wanted to come home – it was a bit of a trek, so I decided to come here.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Did you ever consider any of the other types of engineering at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I nearly did before I got my erm placement at – at college to do a BTec in engineering. I was offered erm an apprenticeship in electronics, erm at – which was sort of connected with another college at home and erm they – and I was like do I want to specialise straight away or do I sort of get a general – and I thought oh I’ll go for a general overview and then it was like sort of umming and aahing about other things, because I nearly considered joining the services as well – doing engineering through them. I was like, oh, I don’t know what to do, you know, so it was sort of a bit up in the air.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you decided to do the BTec, did you know that you wanted to go to university or was it while you were doing that, that you decided?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it was while I was doing it really. Erm, I thought well I can only get so far without a degree, especially in engineering. I was like oh I might as well go and do it then – go to University. But it was quite interesting because it was like – everyone thought oh, you do ‘A’ levels, and then you do – go into University – yeah, so it sort of – and UCAS were in a bit of a nightmare in that sense (really) because they hadn’t not – they’d sort of adapted the UCAS – they’ve got a points system to get in and they’d adapted their system to get into through ‘A’ level students and points and everything like that, and they’d done Scottish highers and everything like that – mention a BTec and they’re like what? Right, well we haven’t a clue how many points for that and so a lot of Universities are like oh, don’t like BTec’s – a bit sort of oh dear.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you ever consider doing ‘A’ levels?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I did, briefly, but I thought I prefer doing course work and I’m not – I thought well I’m not so strong at exams, so I thought well I’ll do – I prefer to do a B – a course work based one – because I didn’t actually have to sit any exams for the BTec.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That sounds good.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, it’s lovely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What is it then, that appeals to you about engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know. (laughs) Erm, I’ve just sort of fallen into it. It’s quite interesting and quite systematic. I like problem solving and things like that. (Yeah) I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s OK. Did you always know that you wanted to do a sandwich course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. Yeah, I thought well erm I’ve got no experience (yeah) of the industry so I was compl – especially on my course, there’s – well, I’m the only one actually doing my degree but there’s sort of 3 other degrees very similar and I was the only – I’m the youngest by about 5 years on it. So the average age is about 35 I’d say, so they’ve all come out of industry, come in doing a degree and then they’ll go back out. And I was like, well, I’m competing against them, at the end of the day, so I thought right…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think the age thing is maybe why the other people haven’t so much (yeah) gone in to doing the placements because they’ve already got that experience?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, and they’ve got families to support and they can’t – they’ve got to get through university as quickly as possible really (Yeah) to erm then be able to go out and back into industry, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, when you decided to do engineering did you realise that it was so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And does it bother you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No it doesn’t. It’s never sort of been an issue. Erm, I mean I was the only – on my – doing the engineering at college, I was the only girl doing that (yeah) and I knew – and it was quite funny because the lect – all the lecturers were like – they were all old school engineers and they’d start swearing and turn around and say what the heck are you doing, sort of thing. And then they’d say, ooh sorry there and they’d apologise to you and I’m like, why? Why are you apologising? And erm I think in some ways it’s like – and they were all – or they’d say oh close your ears Suzanne and have a go. Which I found was quite amusing but in some ways it’s sort of a bit prejudicial – it’s like yeah, I’m no different to them really. Yeah, it was quite funny.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that more women should be encouraged to go into engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely – yeah, because it’s such a big field, I don’t see why it should be so male dominated.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. What do you think could be done to encourage more women into engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Awareness (yeah) it’s more awareness than anything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Knowing what engineering is in the first place?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Exactly because people think engineering – they think car work – mechanical. Erm, and there’s so much more about it that they don’t know about and I mean I had an – I mean – I was at – my school we didn’t really get anything coming through erm and it wasn’t sort of a – oh, you should go and do engineering – people didn’t really think about it, to sort of push the girls through, when I think there is a lot of potential out there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, and do you think that WISE thing was quite crucial for you then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh yeah – I wouldn’t even have thought about it. I was thinking about going and doing law or something like that. I couldn’t sort of imagined doing engineering.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What characteristics do you feel make a good engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think you’ve got to be a sort of quite calm and level headed, erm and systematic in the way you think like problem solving and confident in what they say – yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think any of those characteristics are perceived as more male characteristics or female characteristics?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t think so. I think every – it’s sort of equal – the only thing that I think is erm different, sort of, is the heavy duty sort of eng – is the big, heavy mechanical but if you go through all the degree and everything you’re not likely to go back and do all the heavy manual stuff, it’s more likely to be sort of clean work. (Yes, OK) so that’s the only reason.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there are any particular advantages or disadvantages of being a female engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm, not really. Erm, no. I mean yeah there’s still a lot of people – sort of talking to people there’s still sort of that old school attitude where women aren’t expected to be in engineering and oh no, what’s going on? Erm, I think that’s sort of the only side of it you’ve got to fight against really to get through and prove yourself and you’ve got – in some ways, going – like hitting that in college, it was something that you sort of realised. And you almost have to work twice as hard as the men to show that you’re perfectly capable of doing exactly the same job. I think, in some ways, it pushes you harder so – and so – almost it’s on – if that’s the case everywhere else, that the women are going to end up becoming better than – better quality.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there are any particular advantages to being a woman?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I’ve had some people say that they probably get more help in class and stuff like that (yeah, yeah). I don’t know whether people perceive that as good or patronising or…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, it can come across patronising. I can see where they’re coming across that erm but sometimes it was quite nice, especially being sort of erm in the labs doing lathe work and things like that – I did find it useful then – going, yeah, we’ll come and do it for you (laughs)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, has the course then been what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I’d say yes but it’s totally confused me (yes) because I came in here thinking oh, I’m going to do energy work but there’s quite a lot of environmental and I was a bit sort of prejudicial against it. I was like, oh no, you know, not for me, I’m gonna …and it’s slowly turned me – I’m really confused about what I want to do now. Erm, like I was originally looking for my next year to do a placement within the energy area, sort of energy conservation and things like that erm but I’ve ended up getting a placement in an environmental department (OK). So it’s sort of twisted everything round and I’m like OK, I don’t mind, cos it’s like – I find that I came into the course thinking right I’m gonna come out with an energy based degree and that’s where I’m gonna go – I’m gonna go and work somewhere in that field. And, the environmental thing’s just (sighs) and they said, oh now don’t sort of burn your bridges yet and by the end of the year I was like oh, this environmental stuff isn’t too bad. It’s quite interesting.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK what do you think have been the best and the worse things about the course so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, best things? There’s a (lost words) like the range of subjects we cover (yeah) it is so broad. I mean last year we did erm planning – the planning work, sort of building planning – building regulations and we’ve done like health & safety things and erm, and when we go back sort of environmental technologies – sort of chimney designs and landfill like – so I mean it’s very broad and covers everything and anything (laughs) – it’s quite interesting in that sense, although that can be a disadvantage as well (yeah) because it’s like you can’t – a lot of like a lot of the group you have one sort of area, and they’re all interlocked – we’ll have modules – we’ll have one module and another module sort of miles away – and you’re like OK and…yeah, they sort of overlap but miles sort of very briefly (yeah) so it makes sort of revising it and learning it all very difficult in that sense.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you pleased that you did decide to choose this course then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I am actually. Er, it’s opened my mind up to a lot of things and it’s been very interesting I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s good, have you been taught by any female lecturers at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. Our Law lecturer is female.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So they’re not actually in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, no, they’re in environmental though. Our health – our health & safety lecturer she was – she’s female and she’s engineering based (yeah) and who else, yeah, just those two.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK–do you find that encouraging having female lecturers? Would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I don’t think – it’s like if the subject’s put across in the right way, I don’t see why it should be taught by females…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, so it’s the quality of the teaching staff?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, and if it inspires you to go on, I don’t think it should matter.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s fine. Do you think that the female lecturers treat you the same as the male lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, (yeah?) yeah – there’s no – I wouldn’t say there’s any difference.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And do the male lecturers treat the male and female students the same?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I would say so. You know there’s not – because there’s only like 3 of us, it’s not sort of as it – like at college it was, I was treated slightly different but I had – it was all male lecturers. But here there are like the 3 of us all girls and we’re just treated exactly the same as everyone else.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think you were treated differently at college?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s all because they’re all old school engineers …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And they were like my God it’s a girl, how do we teach a girl?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, they haven’t had like – I was – yeah, I was the only person in the school who they had like at school there, who was a girl. And it was – they were like oh OK. Erm, and then – yeah, then there was a girl in the year below me, who came through but it was sort of a bit – a bit like oh right, yeah, OK, fine…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you got a personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so. (laughs). It’s a bit – because there’s only – there’s only 14 of us on the entire 3 degrees, so – and we – all the lecturers are very approachable, so I think I have somewhere along the line but we – if we’ve got a problem we can go and see any of the lecturers (OK, yes, fine) and any lecturer at any time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anything or anyone that you’d say has been the biggest influence on you, since you started the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you have to do a lot of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, well this year we have – last year we didn’t really have any but this year about half our course work’s been group work, which makes it – it’s been quite difficult because everyone’s old – older. It’s made – and lives away from the University and there’s quite a long distance (yeah) and so getting together and they’ve got all lives at home or they’ve all got jobs outside, so trying to sort of organise group work is just a bit of a nightmare. So, in that sense it’s quite…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah – do you think that there are benefits to doing group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think there is in some ways in the fact that you get an overall view – you get lots of different people’s ideas and you get – you build on everyone else’s strengths and so in a sense you should come out with a decent piece of work at the end. Erm, that’s if everyone pulls their weight.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it will help you when you do go to work in the industry – the fact that you have had the experience of working with other people?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely. Erm, it makes you build on your patience.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you get to choose who you work with when you work in groups, or do you get put into them?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In theory yes, but in practice not really because it sort of all falls into the right – same groups, so it’s not that much of a choice and there’s only a few of us anyway.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely. Yeah, erm, women will put more detail, and more attention to detail rather than the men will just right, that’s it, that’s fine, go. They’re sort of a bit more slapdash erm and a lot of the women have got a lot more patience I always think than certain men.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you prefer working with the women then, or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I dunno, I think it makes it more interesting having a sort of mixed group, because it sort of makes life a bit more challenging.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you had any particularly bad experiences of group work then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I’ve had people not pulling their weight, which is very annoying.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. What do you do in that situation?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Persuade them and then get to the end as sort of deadlines are nearing and it’s like right, OK, fine, we’ll go and do the work ourselves if it’s not going to happen, because at the end of the day it’s your mark that’s being affected, so it’s very annoying when that happens but you have to sort of deal with it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that any aspects of the teaching or advice that you’ve had will help you when you go on your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, obviously like the knowledge that they give us (yeah) but I don’t know – no I …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you will get the opportunity to put the skills that you’ve learnt into practice?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hopefully, yeah. And pick up like lots of new skills as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you feel prepared and ready to go on your placement now?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think so. There’s still a few things that I’ve got to sort out first. Erm, I think yeah – just about getting there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And do the University do anything to help prepare you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, no not really. It’s been sort of they – I’ve had to chase them up to sort of do anything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. How, how much of a role do they have in helping you find a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, in theory they’re meant to have quite – sort of be there, help you and point you in the right direction, but in practice it’s a bit more OK, so go and find it yourself, although my placement actually – the company wrote to the University and it sort of – I was made aware of it (yeah) that they needed someone, so I just applied for it. Erm,

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did anyone particularly encourage or discourage you from going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t think so. I think like erm I talked it over with lecturers and they like sort of said yes, er so they gave me advice on both sides of the sort of – yes, you can finish it early – your degree early – but in my case, because I’ve come straight through, I’ve got no rush to finish it, sort of thing. Erm, I think one thing which is – like for other people who – that puts them off from doing a placement is financial. Erm, they just can’t afford to, but I think it was always going to be a case that I was going to do a placement (yeah) because I knew I had no experience (yeah) so there’s that to think about.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it will improve your career prospects in that respect then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, especially because it’s a big company – an international company. It’s with [company] rm and so it’s a big company and the site is huge and I’ll be working in a team of I think 6. So, in that respect – and they’ve already said, er when I went for my interview they were like well have you done this, have you done that? I was like no, OK we’ll train you up and we’ll show you how to do it. So I’ll get – hopefully, I’ll be able to get lots of experience and they’ve got lots of different things on site, so they’ve got their own landfill site, they’ve got their own incineration plant and things like that and combined heated power unit as well. So there’s lots to sort of pick up on there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And do you have the opportunity to move around within the company?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. I think it will be fairly – cos it’s only – because I’m with the environmental department, it’s going to be fairly restrained but within that – I’ll be able to – I’ll have a year in certain jobs, which is sort of daily jobs and then, but then I’ll be shared between the 6 people so they’ve all got their own little areas, so one’s sort of landfill site – one’s – so I should be able to get a good insight into what goes on and things like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Good. Did you apply to any other companies at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I wrote – who did I write to? I wrote to erm I can’t remember what they’re called now. There’s a Government erm energy saving group, which I wrote to and they said they hadn’t decided on what their budget was so they couldn’t afford to – and then I wrote to a few other people – groups like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What were your main criteria for looking for placements? Was it mainly the type of work they did or did you look, like you said at whether they were willing to train you – did you look at things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really. It was more a case of I needed a placement. I was sort of open to anything by the end of it because I sort of emailed around the companies and there was just nothing (yeah) or they just couldn’t afford to have someone. So, to find a placement was so hard, I was just – I got to the point – cos originally I was like right I’m gonna do energy, I want to do energy (yeah) and it got to the point where I was like well, I don’t mind what I do, if it’s connected. I thought I’ll do it sort of thing. So I was very open in that sense.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Where are they based?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: [Company]? (Yes) Erm, the site which I’m working on is in [town], in [area]. Erm, which is a long way.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, are you worried about that at all or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not really, because it was one question they asked me, is how did I feel being so far away? And I didn’t mind because I worked in the summer – I spent 3 months in Italy working (oh right) so it’s like the distance I don’t mind. As long as there’s a phone sort of thing (yeah) and I can ring home. Erm, but sort of it doesn’t bother me at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you do much research into the company when you… ?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I did before I went for the interview (yeah) because I sort of sent off my CV just as a sort of off chance, so sort of well oh well, I might as well send it off and I hadn’t even a clue what the company was before, it’s a bit bad of me really. And so – and then I had a letter come through saying oh, can you come for interview? I was like what? So I thought I’d better just see what I’ve applied to (laughs) so yeah, a bit of a shock.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that just like looking on the Internet?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, just see what they do. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, would you have liked the University to give you more help in finding a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And what do you think they could have done?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think they could have erm put out more feeders and things (yeah) because I mean yes, we’re only a small group of students but they had about 3 offers, which isn’t a lot.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are any of the males on your course going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think – I think one or two, I’m not sure.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So there’s very few people going on placement anyway, it’s not just girls?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah – it’s not, no. Yeah, I think there’s only about 3 of us, that are out for the year. Erm, so yeah it’s very – it is hard to find them. It’s like looking for a needle in a haystack sometimes and because it’s – like if you were doing mechanics or something like that erm you’d be able to – there’s a lot of placements out there, but you say energy or environmental and they’re like ooh, no we haven’t got anything. It’s very specialised. Yeah, which makes it harder.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what are you most looking forward to and most apprehensive about in placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, looking forward to sort of getting hands on experience, learning the new skills, sort of working within an office environment, which I haven’t done really and working with a sort of team which seems to get on really well. I’ve spoke to the erm the trainee who was there, doing the job at the moment and he was like yeah, they’re really sort of good and they’re really supportive and talking to other people who worked at the company they were like erm yeah, it’s – the company’s really good and they’re really sort of – so I’m looking forward to that sort of support network and how it – so it sort of – and all the different things they’ve got on site, presumably it should be interesting to get into. Erm, apprehensive? Not knowing what sort of – the appropriate information, which is a bit daunt – sort of daunting and a bit – you think oh well, they’re paying me all this money to come here and do the placement, so that’s going to be a bit of a (yeah) – a bit scary in some other senses. Erm, but I’m …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, in terms of your career then what do you see yourself doing in say 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: (laughter) Haven’t got a clue!

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you will you be in the Engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Loosely connected I think. I have a feeling if I really enjoy this placement, I’ll stay in the environmental side and – but it’s still sort of loosely connected because it’s all the technologies and things like that, sort of pollution controls and things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that one of the things that you’re hoping to get out the placement as well? (yeah) … helping you decide more what you want to do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah. Erm, see if I like it – well, fall into something hopefully, but I have a habit of just falling into things. I don’t really plan them it’s like oh yeah, I’ll do that. So I haven’t a clue.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. What would be your ideal career then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Ideal career – erm, I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Not necessarily in terms of a job but erm …

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: What I want to get out of a job sort of thing?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, like do you see yourself going into managerial things or …?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah eventually.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is location and things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, a nice sort of not really urban area, but a sort of semi-urban – a nice location, erm and a nice sort of friendly atmos – company with sort of working within a team, or managerial post – definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that’s achievable?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, eventually (laughs) yeah. A few years experience and then – definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You said that in terms of placement, there isn’t that much going, do you think that the career prospects are good in your field of engineering, or do you think when you come to look for a job do you think you’ll have the same sort of difficulties?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think like jobs – like finding a job – I think there are the jobs out there erm and they are asking for – like if you look in the sort of journals and things (yeah) there are the jobs advertised and – but they’re wanting more than a year’s experience, so in sort of I’ve got to do this placement to be able to get a job at the end. But there are the jobs, it’s just the fact that a lot of companies don’t like doing the – the sort of erm paying for a place for trainees who come through – that’s the sort of impression that I got (yeah) from the different places that I sort of encountered…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you happy with all the career choices you’ve made so far? Would you do anything differently if you had to do it all again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, No, I think it’s sort of – I’ve not been unhappy (yeah) although I probably would have gone to a different college to do the (BTec) BTec – yeah. They were – it’s not the best of places.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: In terms of what?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I was spending my time chasing after lecturers to find where my work – if they’d marked it or – and I was like hang on, I shouldn’t be doing this, they should have it done sort of thing (yeah). They were a bit sort of lax in that sense, which was a bit annoying, especially towards the end. And they didn’t sort of give me the guidance that I needed, it was like erm – well you – like applying through UCAS, it was just – I accidentally found out from a friend, ooh, you’re meant to go and apply through UCAS. I wasn’t told a thing, so in that sense it was sort of – that was my only really bad sort of decision I’d say. But I wouldn’t say no to doing a BTec again.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did any of the other people that were doing your BTec go to University or were they following a different route?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: One – there was one other, but I think he dropped out half way through the first year. Erm, they weren’t academically minded, let’s put it that way. I think they all went into – they all found jobs.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what 5 words would you use to describe sort of your experience of the engineering industry so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I’d say challenging (yeah) – it can be a bit sort of - a bit stand offish to women. Erm, interesting, erm and complicated because there’s so many different fields that it makes it sort of a bit – you go in and say oh, ok I’ll do engineering – what sort? (Yes) You’re definitely not told at school or anything what the difference – there are so many different fields and you say oh engineering – people are like oh right, OK, they think cars again but they’re like – they’re not – kids aren’t informed that there are all these different little pockets, different areas – it’s so wide.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that any of those things might be problematic for you, trying to get into the industry and move forward in the industry, like the fact that it can be stand offish to women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think it will make it more of a challenge but – in some senses – but then it males life a bit more interesting in a sort of – yeah, you’ve got to work, you’ve got to prove yourself a bit more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, does that worry you or bother you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No (laughs) it’s just another challenge. It’s just another difficulty to overcome. So, no, it just makes it interesting.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Why do you think that it’s been so masculine – do you think that’s purely to do with (yes) the numbers of males within the industry or is it the type of work as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s history (yeah). A lot of it has to do with history, that it’s never been a female area and yeah, the number of men in the industry.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think the situation for women will improve?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it will improve very slowly. Erm, it’s just got to sort of gradually pick up the pace a bit. (yeah) But I think it will change in the next sort of 10 to 15 years, I think it will change more and more – become more equal.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK that’s everything. Thanks very much that’s been really helpful.
